compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
At a trade show, either person can follow a script, adapt it to the visitor or give someone time to browse. These choices can reflect training, the visitor’s needs and how busy the booth is.

The shared F and P mean both more often ask first what this means for specific people, and both more often take information in and leave room when dealing with the outside. The difference sits on two axes. One is E/I: does attention and energy go more often to the people and events happening outside, or more often inward, through one's own ideas and feelings first. The other is S/N: does sourcing more often trust observable concrete facts and past experience, or notice connections, patterns and possibility first. Both axes are available; the difference is which side is taken first more often.

Being filed as "the same kind of person" at a trade fair usually happens because the resemblance shows in the most visible places; to separate them, look at which kind of thing each picks up first from the same information.

### The first three seconds at the stand: what the opening line is

In a fictional trade-show example, a visitor pauses at the booth to look at a sample without saying anything. Handing over the sample so they can handle it, or asking what they are looking for, are both available to either type, and the two often come one after the other.

Given the same piece of feedback, the two may attend to different things. The customer says "just looking around". One may care more about whether this unit can show its effect on the spot — judging by feel, output, a live demonstration, the kind of information that can be verified immediately — before deciding how far to go. The other may care more about which usage situations have not been mentioned yet — inferring from what was said, the type of shop, where the visitor is standing, to see whether some possibility has been missed. The first asks "where do you keep this one, and what are you using now", the second asks "which part of your day takes the most time". Both questions are used by both, only more often landing in one place.

Each has a cost. Someone who hands over the sample easily gets filed under "promotion" by a visitor who only wants to see where the industry is going; someone who asks about the situation first may make the other feel interrogated when the guess is wrong, and it takes a moment to bring the conversation back to the product. The size of the cost depends on the footfall that day, who the visitor is and what authority you hold, not on type.

Keep the counterexamples: INFP may push the sample into the visitor's hand with the first sentence, and ESFP may open with "which product are you using now". Which sentence comes at which point, how fast someone speaks and whether the wording is hard or soft can only be used to review the communication strategy you used at the time, not turned around into a type.

### Why Fi and Te are shared while the perceiving pair changes

In the four-function notation used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Both list Fi and Te, in different places: Fi is dominant in INFP and auxiliary in ESFP; Te is third in ESFP and last in INFP. The perceiving side also differs in position: ESFP has Se dominant and Ni inferior, INFP has Ne auxiliary and Si third. This is not the same position renamed; the four positions do not correspond one to one.

The shared labels refer to the same two judging processes in this model. Fi considers personal values, while Te applies criteria and evidence to decisions in the outside world. But with different positions, what can be said is "both may care about this", not "the core is the same", and still less that the two will often agree on whether to take a particular order — that depends on the customer, the conditions and the risk, not on two shared letters.

E/I and S/N say different things and cannot substitute for each other. E and I describe whether attention and energy go outward or inward more often, so one may grow more animated the longer a crowded room goes on, and the other may need to step out and walk a lap; that is not the same as who is warmer. S and N describe whether sourcing trusts concrete facts and experience, or notices connections and possibility faster, so from the same product sheet one may remember the specifications and the sales record first, and the other may think first about where else it could be used. Read the lines separately, and neither person gets summed up as "the livelier one".

The third position is Te for ESFP and Si for INFP; the attitude labelling is not consistent across sources, and this page mentions it only where a distinction needs it, never using a position to infer what someone is good at. The preferences are set out one by one in the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).
compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: what follows are two possible approaches inside the same trade fair and the same family conversation, not a way of deciding by type who should receive visitors or where anyone should be placed. Whether a sale happens depends on the product, the price, the customer's budget and the conditions of the day; type does not enter that judgement.

When the two share a stand, friction tends to appear when one is still handing over a sample and the other has already stepped back half a pace to listen. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first; saying both focuses out loud is usually more useful than arguing about whose approach is more professional.

### The opening line at the fair: who speaks first

(Fictional scene.) The first hour after opening is the busiest, and the two have agreed to take turns greeting. When the first visitor walks over, both hands stop halfway — at that moment either type may hand over the sample, and either may speak first.

Two common approaches. One keeps the person at the stand: "this one arrived in a new colour yesterday, feel it", the sample goes into their hand, and if they respond the conversation carries on. The other looks first for a point of connection: the badge, which unit they are looking at, then "who are you with at the moment", putting the conversation into their situation. The first leans on information that can be verified immediately, the second on possibilities inferred from clues, and both are collecting the same thing: whether the product fits a need the visitor wants to discuss.

The cost depends on conditions. Someone handing over a sample may lose a visitor who only wants to see the trend after two sentences; someone asking about the situation, if the guess is wrong, may make the visitor feel pursued while others queue behind. Which is better value depends on the footfall, who the visitor is and what your role at the stand is, not on type.

A review afterwards is possible, but it targets the wording, not the type: write one line for each opening used that day — what information it relied on, how the visitor responded, and which sentence you would try next time. What is reviewed is which approach travelled better with which customer, not "which type I am". Nor does this record need counting; a few fairs are not a sample that establishes a preference.

### A conversation with a sister: she wants to leave her job and make things by hand

(Fictional scene.) At a family gathering your younger sister says she wants to leave her current job to make things by hand, and asks what you think. Several relatives are at the table, and nobody speaks first.

Either type may ask first what she has in hand: could she try it for three months, how much does a stall at the weekend market cost, how many pieces for a first batch — bringing it down to something she can start on now. Either may also ask first what she feels: is it that you truly like making things, or that you dislike this job — bringing it back to her own wishes. The S/N distinction in this fictional example is between checking concrete information about a trial, such as stall costs and time per item, and exploring possibilities suggested by what she says, such as a part-time trial or a different kind of work. Either person could consider both.

Nor is this about who is more realistic. ESFP may ask first "what do you actually want" and look at the stall afterwards; INFP may calculate the stall fee first, only wanting to confirm before that she is not running away. Both orders can help, and both carry risk: starting with the arithmetic may leave her feeling unheard; starting with motive may leave her feeling interrogated.

To use this conversation for self-observation, write one line afterwards: which of her sentences you caught, whether you relied on checkable numbers or on what her words implied, and which explanations you did not consider. What is written is your own sourcing habit, not a conclusion about her, and certainly not a type decided from a few sentences.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
The first misread is taking INFP's quietness as poor sales ability. How much and how fast someone speaks depends more on experience, the type of customer and the state of the day; a quiet INFP may ask very detailed questions about a customer's situation, and a fast-talking ESFP may realise after the customer leaves that a key need was missed. Judging by "who can sell" gets both wrong.

The second is taking ESFP's liveliness as a lack of depth. What someone cares about is not always said: ESFP's Fi sits in the auxiliary, and they may hold a considered position on how to work together without spelling it out, filtering by action instead; that is not the absence of a standard, and not a lower one.

The third slip is treating talkativeness as evidence about E/I. Someone who talks for eight hours at a fair may be an INFP holding it together; someone sorting samples in a corner may be an ESFP recharging. Recovery style can be used for reflection — do you recover through back-and-forth with people, or through time alone — but it is one clue only: too little sleep, a duty to perform and a customer standing right there all change the day's performance, and a single observation does not establish direction.

The fourth is taking shared letters as "the same core". Both list Fi and Te, but in different positions, and the perceiving side does not correspond either; sharing does not imply the same judgements, nor that one understands the other better.

body: Scope note: what follows are two possible approaches inside the same trade fair and the same family conversation, not a way of deciding by type who should receive visitors or where anyone should be placed. Whether a sale happens depends on the product, the price, the customer's budget and the conditions of the day; type does not enter that judgement.

When the two share a stand, friction tends to appear when one is still handing over a sample and the other has already stepped back half a pace to listen. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first; saying both focuses out loud is usually more useful than arguing about whose approach is more professional.
### The opening line at the fair: who speaks first

(Fictional scene.) The first hour after opening is the busiest, and the two have agreed to take turns greeting. When the first visitor walks over, both hands stop halfway — at that moment either type may hand over the sample, and either may speak first.

Two common approaches. One keeps the person at the stand: "this one arrived in a new colour yesterday, feel it", the sample goes into their hand, and if they respond the conversation carries on. The other looks first for a point of connection: the badge, which unit they are looking at, then "who are you with at the moment", putting the conversation into their situation. The first leans on information that can be verified immediately, the second on possibilities inferred from clues, and both are collecting the same thing: whether the product fits a need the visitor wants to discuss.

The cost depends on conditions. Someone handing over a sample may lose a visitor who only wants to see the trend after two sentences; someone asking about the situation, if the guess is wrong, may make the visitor feel pursued while others queue behind. Which is better value depends on the footfall, who the visitor is and what your role at the stand is, not on type.

A review afterwards is possible, but it targets the wording, not the type: write one line for each opening used that day — what information it relied on, how the visitor responded, and which sentence you would try next time. What is reviewed is which approach travelled better with which customer, not "which type I am". Nor does this record need counting; a few fairs are not a sample that establishes a preference.
### A conversation with a sister: she wants to leave her job and make things by hand

(Fictional scene.) At a family gathering your younger sister says she wants to leave her current job to make things by hand, and asks what you think. Several relatives are at the table, and nobody speaks first.

Either type may ask first what she has in hand: could she try it for three months, how much does a stall at the weekend market cost, how many pieces for a first batch — bringing it down to something she can start on now. Either may also ask first what she feels: is it that you truly like making things, or that you dislike this job — bringing it back to her own wishes. The S/N distinction in this fictional example is between checking concrete information about a trial, such as stall costs and time per item, and exploring possibilities suggested by what she says, such as a part-time trial or a different kind of work. Either person could consider both.

Nor is this about who is more realistic. ESFP may ask first "what do you actually want" and look at the stall afterwards; INFP may calculate the stall fee first, only wanting to confirm before that she is not running away. Both orders can help, and both carry risk: starting with the arithmetic may leave her feeling unheard; starting with motive may leave her feeling interrogated.

What is written is your own sourcing habit, not a conclusion about her, and certainly not a type decided from a few sentences.

body: The first misread is taking INFP's quietness as poor sales ability. How much and how fast someone speaks depends more on experience, the type of customer and the state of the day; a quiet INFP may ask very detailed questions about a customer's situation, and a fast-talking ESFP may realise after the customer leaves that a key need was missed. Judging by "who can sell" gets both wrong.

The second is taking ESFP's liveliness as a lack of depth. What someone cares about is not always said: ESFP's Fi sits in the auxiliary, and they may hold a considered position on how to work together without spelling it out, filtering by action instead; that is not the absence of a standard, and not a lower one.

The third slip is treating talkativeness as evidence about E/I. Someone who talks for eight hours at a fair may be an INFP holding it together; someone sorting samples in a corner may be an ESFP recharging. Recovery style can be used for reflection — do you recover through back-and-forth with people, or through time alone — but it is one clue only: too little sleep, a duty to perform and a customer standing right there all change the day's performance, and a single observation does not establish direction.

The fourth is taking shared letters as "the same core". Both list Fi and Te, but in different positions, and the perceiving side does not correspond either; sharing does not imply the same judgements, nor that one understands the other better.

items.answer:
Both can. INFP may be surprisingly forward in a familiar industry, and ESFP may think all evening about a customer's offhand remark.

items.question: INFP can be warm on the spot, and ESFP can replay one sentence all evening?

items.answer:
Not in who speaks first, but in what is relied on: one may take the facts verifiable on the spot — who came by, how the sample feels, which model has been asked about most; the other may take the situation inferred from clues — where they stopped, what the badge says, what the last sentence hinted at.

items.question: Standing at a stand and introducing yourself — where is the difference?

items.answer:
Not by type. The practical split is by experience and authority: whoever knows this product line better presents; whoever is better at drawing out concerns follows up; whoever has other customers waiting takes the details and the later contact.

They can also alternate: one opens the conversation and puts the sample in the visitor's hand, the other draws out the real concern once the customer sits down, and the reverse works as well. What to avoid is competing for the same moment — one still reading the visitor's face while the other has already quoted a price leaves the customer feeling pushed. faq_blocks.question: What is most easily confused between ESFP and INFP?

faq_blocks.answer:
In the common four-function notation used here, both list Fi and Te, in different places: Fi is dominant in INFP and auxiliary in ESFP; Te is third in ESFP and last in INFP. ESFP's perceiving is Se dominant with Ni inferior; INFP's is Ne auxiliary with Si third.

body: At a trade show, either person can follow a script, adapt it to the visitor or give someone time to browse. These choices can reflect training, the visitor’s needs and how busy the booth is.

The shared F and P mean both more often ask first what this means for specific people, and both more often take information in and leave room when dealing with the outside. The difference sits on two axes. One is E/I: does attention and energy go more often to the people and events happening outside, or more often inward, through one's own ideas and feelings first. The other is S/N: does sourcing more often trust observable concrete facts and past experience, or notice connections, patterns and possibility first. Both axes are available; the difference is which side is taken first more often.

Being filed as "the same kind of person" at a trade fair usually happens because the resemblance shows in the most visible places; to separate them, look at which kind of thing each picks up first from the same information.
### The first three seconds at the stand: what the opening line is

In a fictional trade-show example, a visitor pauses at the booth to look at a sample without saying anything. Handing over the sample so they can handle it, or asking what they are looking for, are both available to either type, and the two often come one after the other.

Given the same piece of feedback, the two may attend to different things. The customer says "just looking around". One may care more about whether this unit can show its effect on the spot — judging by feel, output, a live demonstration, the kind of information that can be verified immediately — before deciding how far to go. The other may care more about which usage situations have not been mentioned yet — inferring from what was said, the type of shop, where the visitor is standing, to see whether some possibility has been missed. The first asks "where do you keep this one, and what are you using now", the second asks "which part of your day takes the most time". Both questions are used by both, only more often landing in one place.

Each has a cost. Someone who hands over the sample easily gets filed under "promotion" by a visitor who only wants to see where the industry is going; someone who asks about the situation first may make the other feel interrogated when the guess is wrong, and it takes a moment to bring the conversation back to the product. The size of the cost depends on the footfall that day, who the visitor is and what authority you hold, not on type.

Keep the counterexamples: INFP may push the sample into the visitor's hand with the first sentence, and ESFP may open with "which product are you using now". Which sentence comes at which point, how fast someone speaks and whether the wording is hard or soft can only be used to review the communication strategy you used at the time, not turned around into a type.
### Why Fi and Te are shared while the perceiving pair changes

In the four-function notation used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Both list Fi and Te, in different places: Fi is dominant in INFP and auxiliary in ESFP; Te is third in ESFP and last in INFP. The perceiving side also differs in position: ESFP has Se dominant and Ni inferior, INFP has Ne auxiliary and Si third. This is not the same position renamed; the four positions do not correspond one to one.

The shared labels refer to the same two judging processes in this model. Fi considers personal values, while Te applies criteria and evidence to decisions in the outside world. But with different positions, what can be said is "both may care about this", not "the core is the same", and still less that the two will often agree on whether to take a particular order — that depends on the customer, the conditions and the risk, not on two shared letters.

E/I and S/N say different things and cannot substitute for each other. E and I describe whether attention and energy go outward or inward more often, so one may grow more animated the longer a crowded room goes on, and the other may need to step out and walk a lap; that is not the same as who is warmer. S and N describe whether sourcing trusts concrete facts and experience, or notices connections and possibility faster, so from the same product sheet one may remember the specifications and the sales record first, and the other may think first about where else it could be used. Read the lines separately, and neither person gets summed up as "the livelier one".

The third position is Te for ESFP and Si for INFP; the attitude labelling is not consistent across sources, and this page mentions it only where a distinction needs it, never using a position to infer what someone is good at. The preferences are set out one by one in the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
At a trade show, either person can follow a script, adapt it to the visitor or give someone time to browse. These choices can reflect training, the visitor’s needs and how busy the booth is.

The shared F and P mean both more often ask first what this means for specific people, and both more often take information in and leave room when dealing with the outside. The difference sits on two axes. One is E/I: does attention and energy go more often to the people and events happening outside, or more often inward, through one's own ideas and feelings first. The other is S/N: does sourcing more often trust observable concrete facts and past experience, or notice connections, patterns and possibility first. Both axes are available; the difference is which side is taken first more often.

Being filed as "the same kind of person" at a trade fair usually happens because the resemblance shows in the most visible places; to separate them, look at which kind of thing each picks up first from the same information.

### The first three seconds at the stand: what the opening line is

In a fictional trade-show example, a visitor pauses at the booth to look at a sample without saying anything. Handing over the sample so they can handle it, or asking what they are looking for, are both available to either type, and the two often come one after the other.

Given the same piece of feedback, the two may attend to different things. The customer says "just looking around". One may care more about whether this unit can show its effect on the spot — judging by feel, output, a live demonstration, the kind of information that can be verified immediately — before deciding how far to go. The other may care more about which usage situations have not been mentioned yet — inferring from what was said, the type of shop, where the visitor is standing, to see whether some possibility has been missed. The first asks "where do you keep this one, and what are you using now", the second asks "which part of your day takes the most time". Both questions are used by both, only more often landing in one place.

Each has a cost. Someone who hands over the sample easily gets filed under "promotion" by a visitor who only wants to see where the industry is going; someone who asks about the situation first may make the other feel interrogated when the guess is wrong, and it takes a moment to bring the conversation back to the product. The size of the cost depends on the footfall that day, who the visitor is and what authority you hold, not on type.

Keep the counterexamples: INFP may push the sample into the visitor's hand with the first sentence, and ESFP may open with "which product are you using now". Which sentence comes at which point, how fast someone speaks and whether the wording is hard or soft can only be used to review the communication strategy you used at the time, not turned around into a type.

### Why Fi and Te are shared while the perceiving pair changes

In the four-function notation used here, ESFP is Se–Fi–Te–Ni and INFP is Fi–Ne–Si–Te. Both list Fi and Te, in different places: Fi is dominant in INFP and auxiliary in ESFP; Te is third in ESFP and last in INFP. The perceiving side also differs in position: ESFP has Se dominant and Ni inferior, INFP has Ne auxiliary and Si third. This is not the same position renamed; the four positions do not correspond one to one.

The shared labels refer to the same two judging processes in this model. Fi considers personal values, while Te applies criteria and evidence to decisions in the outside world. But with different positions, what can be said is "both may care about this", not "the core is the same", and still less that the two will often agree on whether to take a particular order — that depends on the customer, the conditions and the risk, not on two shared letters.

E/I and S/N say different things and cannot substitute for each other. E and I describe whether attention and energy go outward or inward more often, so one may grow more animated the longer a crowded room goes on, and the other may need to step out and walk a lap; that is not the same as who is warmer. S and N describe whether sourcing trusts concrete facts and experience, or notices connections and possibility faster, so from the same product sheet one may remember the specifications and the sales record first, and the other may think first about where else it could be used. Read the lines separately, and neither person gets summed up as "the livelier one".

The third position is Te for ESFP and Si for INFP; the attitude labelling is not consistent across sources, and this page mentions it only where a distinction needs it, never using a position to infer what someone is good at. The preferences are set out one by one in the [ESFP profile](/en/personality/esfp) and the [INFP profile](/en/personality/infp).

sections.title: ESFP and INFP in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: what follows are two possible approaches inside the same trade fair and the same family conversation, not a way of deciding by type who should receive visitors or where anyone should be placed. Whether a sale happens depends on the product, the price, the customer's budget and the conditions of the day; type does not enter that judgement.

When the two share a stand, friction tends to appear when one is still handing over a sample and the other has already stepped back half a pace to listen. It is rarely about who is right, but about which kind of information each handles first; saying both focuses out loud is usually more useful than arguing about whose approach is more professional.

### The opening line at the fair: who speaks first

(Fictional scene.) The first hour after opening is the busiest, and the two have agreed to take turns greeting. When the first visitor walks over, both hands stop halfway — at that moment either type may hand over the sample, and either may speak first.

Two common approaches. One keeps the person at the stand: "this one arrived in a new colour yesterday, feel it", the sample goes into their hand, and if they respond the conversation carries on. The other looks first for a point of connection: the badge, which unit they are looking at, then "who are you with at the moment", putting the conversation into their situation. The first leans on information that can be verified immediately, the second on possibilities inferred from clues, and both are collecting the same thing: whether the product fits a need the visitor wants to discuss.

The cost depends on conditions. Someone handing over a sample may lose a visitor who only wants to see the trend after two sentences; someone asking about the situation, if the guess is wrong, may make the visitor feel pursued while others queue behind. Which is better value depends on the footfall, who the visitor is and what your role at the stand is, not on type.

A review afterwards is possible, but it targets the wording, not the type: write one line for each opening used that day — what information it relied on, how the visitor responded, and which sentence you would try next time. What is reviewed is which approach travelled better with which customer, not "which type I am". Nor does this record need counting; a few fairs are not a sample that establishes a preference.

### A conversation with a sister: she wants to leave her job and make things by hand

(Fictional scene.) At a family gathering your younger sister says she wants to leave her current job to make things by hand, and asks what you think. Several relatives are at the table, and nobody speaks first.

Either type may ask first what she has in hand: could she try it for three months, how much does a stall at the weekend market cost, how many pieces for a first batch — bringing it down to something she can start on now. Either may also ask first what she feels: is it that you truly like making things, or that you dislike this job — bringing it back to her own wishes. The S/N distinction in this fictional example is between checking concrete information about a trial, such as stall costs and time per item, and exploring possibilities suggested by what she says, such as a part-time trial or a different kind of work. Either person could consider both.

Nor is this about who is more realistic. ESFP may ask first "what do you actually want" and look at the stall afterwards; INFP may calculate the stall fee first, only wanting to confirm before that she is not running away. Both orders can help, and both carry risk: starting with the arithmetic may leave her feeling unheard; starting with motive may leave her feeling interrogated.

To use this conversation for self-observation, write one line afterwards: which of her sentences you caught, whether you relied on checkable numbers or on what her words implied, and which explanations you did not consider. What is written is your own sourcing habit, not a conclusion about her, and certainly not a type decided from a few sentences.

sections.body_md:
The first misread is taking INFP's quietness as poor sales ability. How much and how fast someone speaks depends more on experience, the type of customer and the state of the day; a quiet INFP may ask very detailed questions about a customer's situation, and a fast-talking ESFP may realise after the customer leaves that a key need was missed. Judging by "who can sell" gets both wrong.

The second is taking ESFP's liveliness as a lack of depth. What someone cares about is not always said: ESFP's Fi sits in the auxiliary, and they may hold a considered position on how to work together without spelling it out, filtering by action instead; that is not the absence of a standard, and not a lower one.

The third slip is treating talkativeness as evidence about E/I. Someone who talks for eight hours at a fair may be an INFP holding it together; someone sorting samples in a corner may be an ESFP recharging. Recovery style can be used for reflection — do you recover through back-and-forth with people, or through time alone — but it is one clue only: too little sleep, a duty to perform and a customer standing right there all change the day's performance, and a single observation does not establish direction.

The fourth is taking shared letters as "the same core". Both list Fi and Te, but in different positions, and the perceiving side does not correspond either; sharing does not imply the same judgements, nor that one understands the other better.
